passage:
The power had gone out, and Shalini was bathing five-year-old Pranav by torchlight, hurrying before the water went cold.
"Remember our rule?" she asked, pouring a mug over his head.
"My swimsuit parts are private!" Pranav shouted.
"And if any grown-up says, let's keep a secret from Mummy?"
"I tell you anyway!"
"Even if it's someone nice? Even if they give you chocolate?"
Pranav thought, dripping. "Even then. Surprises okay. Secrets no."
Shalini wrapped him in the towel. "And you'll never be in trouble for telling. Never."

qa.q: Why was Shalini bathing Pranav by torchlight?
qa.a: The power had gone out.

qa.q: How might Pranav feel about the rule, judging by his shout?
qa.a: He seems proud and confident, shouting the rule because he knows it well and it feels like a game, not something scary.

qa.q: What part of Shalini's teaching helps most?
qa.a: Repeating simple rules calmly and promising he will never be in trouble for telling makes it easy for Pranav to speak up.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini taught the rule by scaring Pranav?
qa.a: Pranav might feel anxious or ashamed and be less likely to tell her things, while the calm game makes telling feel safe.

grounding: A mother uses a hurried bath time to repeat simple body-privacy and no-secrets rules with her five-year-old, and promises he will never be in trouble for telling.

passage:
In the kindergarten room, Urmila Miss held up a sock puppet named Chintu.
"Chintu's neighbour said, don't tell your Amma I gave you sweets. Our secret. What should Chintu do?"
Naveen, five, stood on his chair. "Tell Amma!"
"Yes! Grown-ups should never ask children to keep secrets from their parents. And whose body is private?"
"Mine!" the class shouted.
Naveen frowned. "Miss, my Mama is hiding a cake for Amma's birthday. Is that bad?"
Urmila Miss smiled. "That's a surprise. Surprises are happy, and everyone finds out soon. Secrets that feel yucky, you tell."
Naveen made Chintu clap.

qa.q: What was the sock puppet's name?
qa.a: The sock puppet was named Chintu.

qa.q: Why did Naveen frown and ask about the cake?
qa.a: He was worried that keeping Mama's cake hidden might be bad, because it sounded like the secret in the rule.

qa.q: How did Urmila Miss help the class tell secrets from surprises?
qa.a: She explained simply that surprises are happy and everyone finds out soon, while secrets that feel yucky should always be told.

qa.q: How might Naveen's Amma feel hearing about this lesson?
qa.a: She might feel reassured that Naveen knows he can always tell her things, and that the lesson was gentle, not frightening.

grounding: A kindergarten teacher uses a puppet and simple repeated rules to teach young children that bodies are private and that yucky secrets are always told.

passage:
"Usha, bath time talk," Mummy said, wrapping her in a towel.
"Again?"
"Again. What are the parts your swimsuit covers?"
"Private!" said Usha.
"And who can touch them?"
"Nobody. Only doctor, if Mummy is there."
"Good. And if any grown-up says, 'Don't tell Mummy'?"
Usha thought. "I tell Mummy."
"Even if it's someone you like?"
"Even then."
"What about surprises, like a birthday gift?"
"Surprises are okay. Secrets are not."
Mahima kissed her wet head. "You can always tell me anything. I'll never be angry at you for telling."
Usha nodded and splashed.

qa.q: Who can touch Usha's private parts, according to Usha?
qa.a: Nobody. Only doctor, if Mummy is there.

qa.q: What does Mahima seem to feel as she kisses Usha's wet head?
qa.a: Mahima seems loving and protective, calm rather than fearful, wanting Usha to feel safe telling her anything.

qa.q: What did Mahima do well to keep Usha safe?
qa.a: She repeated simple rules gently, explained surprises versus secrets, and promised Usha she would never be angry at her for telling.

qa.q: How might Usha feel if something worrying happened one day?
qa.a: Usha would likely feel safer telling Mummy, because she knows the rule and knows she won't be scolded.

grounding: It shows a mother teaching her young child simple body-safety and no-secrets rules calmly and repeatedly, without fear.

passage:
Preschool note to parents, Friday. From Neelam, class teacher.
Our new body safety song goes: "My body is mine. My private parts are private. If something feels wrong, I tell."
At circle time, Nazia asked, "What if an uncle says it's a secret?"
I said, "Surprises, like a birthday cake, are fine. But no grown-up should ask you to keep a secret from Mumma or Papa. If they do, tell a grown-up you trust."
Nazia nodded. "Then I tell Ammi."
We practised it calmly, like brushing teeth. Please sing it at home too.

qa.q: What did Nazia ask during circle time?
qa.a: "What if an uncle says it's a secret?"

qa.q: How did Nazia seem to feel after the teacher's answer?
qa.a: Nazia seemed reassured and clear, nodding and deciding she would tell Ammi.

qa.q: What did the teacher ask parents to do?
qa.a: Sing the song at home too.

qa.q: How might the other children feel practising the song calmly?
qa.a: They would likely feel safe and confident, since the rules are practised like brushing teeth, not taught with fear.

grounding: A preschool teacher teaches simple body-safety and no-secrets rules calmly, answering a child's question about secrets from adults.

passage:
In the courtyard of their village home, Binita oiled little Anirban's hair.
"Tell me the rule," she said.
"My body is mine," Anirban said. "Nobody touches where my chaddi is."
"Good. And if someone says, 'Don't tell your Ma'?"
"I tell Ma. Fast fast."
"And if you're scared to tell?"
"You won't be angry."
"Never." Binita kissed his oily forehead. "Some secrets are fun, like hiding Baba's birthday sweets. But nobody should ask you to hide things from me."
Anirban grinned. "Baba's sweets are in the steel box."
"Shh! That one is a surprise."

qa.q: Where were Binita and Anirban sitting?
qa.a: In the courtyard of their village home.

qa.q: How does Anirban feel when saying the rules?
qa.a: Anirban feels relaxed and confident, grinning and joking, because the rules are familiar and gentle.

qa.q: How did Binita teach body safety without fear?
qa.a: She used simple repeated rules, explained that she would never be angry, and showed the difference between a fun surprise and a secret.

qa.q: How might Binita feel as she teaches the rule?
qa.a: Binita feels loving and protective, wanting Anirban to know he can always tell her.

grounding: It shows a village mother teaching her small son simple body-safety and no-secrets rules warmly and without fear.

passage: At the kindergarten in Busan, Ms Leila sat the children on the rug beside a drawing of a child in a swimsuit. "The parts under your swimsuit are private," she said. "Nobody should touch them or ask to see them." Soo-ah raised her hand. "Not even a nice grown-up?" "Not even a nice one. And a grown-up should never ask you to keep a secret from Mum or Dad. Surprises, like a birthday present, are fine, because everyone finds out soon." They practised saying, "No! I'm telling!" in big voices. Soo-ah shouted loudest, then giggled.

qa.q: What did the children practise saying?
qa.a: They practised saying “No! I'm telling!” in big voices.

qa.q: How did Soo-ah seem to feel while practising?
qa.a: Soo-ah seemed confident and cheerful, shouting loudest and then giggling, so the rule felt safe rather than scary.

qa.q: Why is teaching the rules with practice better than frightening stories?
qa.a: Simple rules repeated and practised playfully help children remember what to do and whom to tell, without making them afraid.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah's parents feel hearing about the lesson?
qa.a: They might feel reassured and grateful, knowing Soo-ah learned that grown-ups should not ask for secrets from Mum or Dad and that telling is always allowed.

grounding: Shows an adult teaching young children that private parts are private, that grown-ups should not ask for secrets from parents, and that telling is always allowed.
